blocks.text: V. The last passage on the basilisk is Ierem. VIII, 17. For I will send among you serpents, basilisks, against which there is no charm, and they shall bite you, says the Lord. Here the Chaldee has: For I will stir up against you עממיא קטולין כחוין חרמנין דלית להון לחשא, murderous peoples, like serpents, reguli, against which there is no charm. Theodoret understands this of enemies who ταῖς ἡμετέραις οὐκ εἴκουσι παρακλήσεσιν [tais hēmeterais ouk eikousi paraklēsesin], do not yield to our entreaties; Jerome understands it of the ancient serpent and of the hostile powers to whom those who have despised God's commandments will be handed over. We prefer to understand it of the Assyrians, to whom the Israelites were soon to be handed over. In place of basilisks the second edition had σκοποὺς [skopous], watchmen, that is, צפים instead of צפענים. R. Selomo idly claims that any serpent, once it has lived seventy years, becomes a צפע, a basilisk, and then stops its ear so as not to hear the charmer. He proves this from Psal. LVIII, 5., where, however, there is nothing about the צפע or basilisk. Rather, what we read there is that the פתן, the asp, stops its ear ^{d)}, etc., which has been fully explained above ^{e)}.
